content: 1. Tools and registers in maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH) programs facilitate cohort monitoring of maternal antiretroviral therapy (ART) retention and the retention of HIV-exposed infants in care. 2. Pregnant and breastfeeding women who initiate ART in MNCH settings are included in both site-level and national-level ART monitoring and evaluation (M&E) systems. 3. Systems are in place to track and measure the linkages and transitions between MNCH services and long-term HIV care and treatment for both mothers and infants. Examples include mother-baby longitudinal registries and the use of unique identifiers. 4. Program evaluations are designed to identify early successes and challenges, as well as to assess long-term maternal and infant outcomes, including the prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV. 5. Routine data quality assurance processes are implemented to ensure the accuracy and reliability of collected data. 6. Efforts are made to harmonize prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) and ART M&E systems, as well as data review processes. 7. Standardized files or cards are used for pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV and their HIV-exposed infants to ensure consistent documentation. 8. Routine site supervision and clinical mentoring are conducted to maintain the quality of care provided. 9. Continuous quality improvement processes are implemented for PMTCT programs to enhance service delivery. 10. HIV testing and counseling (HTC) in PMTCT settings include quality assurance measures for rapid HIV testing at all PMTCT sites. 11. Policies are established regarding the treatment of discordant couples (where one partner is HIV-positive and the other is HIV-negative). 12. Couples HTC and follow-up for discordant couples are incorporated into PMTCT strategies. 13. Strategies are developed to link or register male partners living with HIV into ART programs. 14. Counseling on ART initiation and adherence includes specialized messaging and support services for pregnant and breastfeeding women starting ART. 15. Structures are established to expedite preparation for ART initiation. 16. Alternative protocols are developed for women who do not require ART for their own health but decline lifelong treatment. 17. Laboratory and clinical monitoring capabilities include systems for monitoring treatment toxicity and the availability of baseline CD4 testing (via point-of-care or reliable sample transport). 18. Algorithms are developed for CD4 and/or viral load monitoring to guide clinical decision-making. 19. Early infant diagnosis (EID) capacity is scaled up in parallel with PMTCT program expansion. 20. The EID cascade is strengthened to ensure early diagnosis, rapid return of results, active case finding of HIV-infected infants, and timely initiation of treatment. 21. Retention of HIV-exposed infants through the end of breastfeeding is prioritized, including ensuring final diagnosis. 22. Access to pediatric HIV treatment is expanded to meet the needs of children living with HIV. 23. Systems are established to ensure that all pregnant and postpartum women living with HIV are enrolled in ongoing HIV care and/or treatment. 24. Models of service delivery are developed to harmonize mother-infant pair follow-up. 25. Facilityand community-based services are implemented to support ART adherence and trace defaulters. 26. Innovative solutions are explored to improve the accessibility of ART for women and children. 27. Family planning services are assessed for availability and the adequacy of commodities. 28. Access to and uptake of voluntary family planning services are promoted in settings providing ART. 29. Women living with HIV are actively engaged in the planning, implementation, and monitoring of programs at national, subnational, and community levels. 30. Community-based activities and services are implemented to support PMTCT scale-up and retention in care. 31. Community structures are established to support orphans and vulnerable children affected by HIV. 32. Roll-out strategies for ART programs are planned, including real-time evaluation of implementation to inform further scale-up. 33. Simplified dosing guidelines for antiretroviral drugs are developed to ensure safe and effective treatment for children. 34. Fixed-dose combination formulations are preferred for children, and efforts are made to avoid oral liquid formulations where possible. 35. Dispersible tablets are recommended as the preferred solid oral dosage form for children, as they can be converted into liquid at the point of use. 36. Children are weighed at each clinic visit, and dose adjustments are made as they grow or gain weight. 37. Adult formulations may be used for children when necessary, but care must be taken to avoid underdosing. 38. Tablets that are not easily split should be divided at the dispensing pharmacy using appropriate tools. 39. Heat-stable formulations, such as lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) tablets, must not be split or crushed, as this compromises bioavailability. 40. The Pediatric Antiretroviral Working Group highlights the urgent need for new formulations, including fixed-dose combinations suitable for younger children and heat-stable formulations for use in resource-limited settings. 41. Simplified prescribing, dispensing, and dosing guidance is regularly updated as new data and formulations become available. 42. National programs are advised to ensure that all procured products meet appropriate quality and stability standards. 43. The WHO continues to work with pharmaceutical companies and other partners to develop practical recommendations and formulations to accelerate ART scale-up for children.
